Self-Aligned, Emitter-Edge-Passivated AIGaAs/GaAs Heterojunction Bipolar Transistors with Extrapolated Maximum Oscillation Frequency of 350 GHz
abstract: This work presents self-aligned, emitter-edge-passivated AlGaAs/GaAs heterojunction bipolar transistors with extrapolated maximum oscillation frequency of 350 GHz. To our knowledge, this is the highest fmax ever reported for an HBT. In the past, fmax of 218 GHz has been demonstrated for devices fabricated using the self-aligned dual liftoff process(l). This self-aligned structure reduces the base resistance and base collector capacitance. However, the de current gain was relatively low (l0-12) because there was no emitter-edge-passivation to reduce surface recombination at the emitter periphery. In this paper a self-aligned, emitter-edge-passivated dual liftoff process is reported, which enhances the device RF performance and dc current gain.

Monolithic high power millimeter wave quasi-optical frequency multiplier arrays using quantum barrier devices
abstract: Monolithic solid state device arrays are under development for application as millimeter and submillimeter sources. Current efforts are focused on frequency multiplication up to approximately equal to 100 GHz at the 1-50 W power level. However, the intrinsic capabilities of several of the devices should permit the extension of this work to frequencies of several THz. GaAs barrier-N-N+ (BNN) diode arrays have been successfully designed and fabricated. Frequency doubling to 66 GHz has been successfully achieved with an output power of 2.4-2.6 W and an efficiency in excess of 10%. In addition to the BNN arrays, a number of new device concepts have been developed in the course of this research which offer the promise of more efficient frequency multipliers with both higher cutoff frequency and higher power handling capability. These include the multi-quantum-barrier-varactor (MQBV), and the Schottky-quantum-barrier-varactor (SQBV).

abstract: This conference was the first technical forum to hear of the transistor. Although subsequent advances were shared with other conferences, many of them its offspring, the Device Research Conference was the leader for classic semiconductor devices, from the point contact transistor and the photodiode to the farthest limits of integration and the charge-coupled area imager. Its spirit of sharing knowledge so as to achieve shared and rapid technical advance permeated the field for many years. The openness advocated and practiced by Jack A. Morton and the Bell Laboratories was followed by breath-taking technology changes, a majority of them from Bell Laboratories. Structures and theory went from basic junction to space charge layer widening to high level injection to the drift transistor, this conceived before its time by a young German theorist at Darmstadt. The heterojunction and ion implanted structures were proposed. Germanium grown junctions were followed by germanium alloy transistors, a technology still practiced commercially here at Boston. The surface barrier transistor was followed by the micro-alloy transistor. Diffused transistors appeared in germanium and silicon and the diffusion approach was grafted onto existing manufactures of grown junction devices and alloy devices, with the microalloy diffused transistor (MADT) enjoying a brief moment in the spotlight of performance before being washed away by the use of epitaxial substrates in mesa and planar devices. Then the silicon integrated circuit with its reverse bias insulation, integral Si02 insulation, and adherent aluminum wiring appeared and the world was transformed again. At the same time as epitaxy and the integrated circuit, the MOS transistor came out. rapidly followed (in consequence of prodigious efforts) by CMOS circuits. Then. very late, long after a transit time semiconductor device was proven impractical, the charge-coupled device emerged and to dominate the photosensing world. In all this. processing was key, with single crystal growth most fundamental. diffusion ubiquitous and unavoidable. and oxide masking and photolithography astonishing in their capability for geometric down-scaling. Ion implantation came to improve control and to permit new subtleties of structure. Nature is in such balance that the properties of silicon are as desirable as they seem improbable. Energy gap, impurity solubilities and diffusion constants. carrier mobilities and lifetimes, surface state densities let wild dreams become realities.

abstract: We report the first unambiguous demonstration that ternary quantum well intersub-band transitions are TE, as well as TM, active, a result that has significant implications for the applications of these transitions in a variety of infrared detector structures. Using a unique waveguide measurement geometry, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) absorption measurements have been made on a number of lattice-matched In<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.53</sub>Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.47</sub>As/In<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.52</sub>Al<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.48</sub>As and strained In<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.7</sub>Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.3</sub>As/AlAs/In<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.52</sub>Al<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.48</sub>/In<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.53</sub>Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.47</sub>As single quantum well waveguide heterostructures. These measurements show that both TE and TM polarized light can excite intersubband transitions, whereas the conventional wisdom is that these transitions are only sensitive to TM polarized light. The realization that these transitions are also TE active results in significant simplifications in the design of infrared detectors based on exploiting intersubband transitions.

Hydrogenation effects on polysilicon thin film transistor structures
abstract: Polysilicon thin film transistors (TFTs) have potential applications in Active Matrix Liquid Crystal Displays and Static Random Access Memories. It is well known that these devices improve after a hydrogen plasma anneal. In this work, we have investigated the hydrogenation of various polysilicon TFT structures in a parallel plate reactor and studied the effect of plasma frequency (30 kHz or 13.56 MHz) on the device characteristics. The device structures included a) nonself- aligned metal gate, b) self-aligned polysilicon gate, and c) offset polysilicon gate. Both polysilicon and metal gate structures improved after the hydrogenation at 30 kHz. The subthreshold slope of polysilicon gate TFTs was by a factor of two lower than that of metal gate showing that the polysilicon gate results in a more efficient hydrogenation of the device structure. The hydrogenation at 13.56 MHz either marginally improve the devices or under certain conditions actually degrade them. To further confirm the incorporation of positive hydrogen ions in the dielectric during the high frequency hydrogenation, we characterized n+-i-n+ and p+-i-p+ polysilicon resistors. The effect of high frequency hydrogenation on n-channel polysilicon TFTs having an offset gate structure was then investigated. These devices do not exhibit an anomalous leakage current; however, due to the high series resistance of the offset region the device ON current is degraded.

articleTitle: Time resolved investigations of field screening in InGaAs/InGaAIAs and InGaAs/InGaAsP multiple quantum wrll devices
abstract: Integrated high-speed intensity modulators based on the quantum confined stark effect (QCSE) are highly attractive devices for optical communication systems. We investigated two different important well/barrier material combinations suitable for long-wavelength modulators, namely, InGaAs/InGaAsP and InGaAs/InGaAlAs. We show that the difference in the band discontinuities between the two material systems has a large influence on modulator performance. We used a combined theoretical and experimental approach to evaluate this difference. A carrier transport model was developed which includes tunneling between wells, transfer to confinement layers, recombination and thermionic emission. With this model the carrier population of the wells and the internal field within the device after optical carrier injection was calculated. The absolute change of the internal field after pulsed excitation and the speed of recovery back to the external field shows the sensitivity of the modulator to incoming light. The structures studied consisted of five l0nm InGaAs quantum wells separated by 5nm barriers of either InGaAsP or InGaAlAs with 100 nm of linear confinement layers each side of the quantum well regions. The bandgap of the barrier and confinement layers was 1.3μm . The structures were grown on n-doped substrates and had p-doped contact layers. We conclude that InGaAs/InGaAsP quantum wells are more suitable for QCSE modulator than are InGaAs/InGaAlAs devices.

A New Family of Gaseous Sensors UtiIizing Catalyst - Adsorptive Oxide MIS Structure
abstract: A new family of gaseous sensors utilizing Catalyst - Adsorptive Oxide - Semiconductor MIS Structure fabricated on silicon has been developed for gases detection. Devices with Pd, Pt, or Ag as catalyst layer deposited on highly resistive SnOx, or ZnO adsorptive oxide incorporated in the MIS capacitor have been studied for the detection of O2, H2, and CO gases. The operating principle of the devices is based on the change in ionic charge density and/or charge redistribution in the adsorptive oxide, SnOx or ZnO of the MIS capacitor upon gases adsorption. This leads to a shift in the flat-band voltage of the device. The mechanism of Oz detection is attributed to the dissociation of Oz molecules on the metal catalyst and the subsequent chemisorption at extrinsic surface states in the adsorptive oxide as negatively charged ions. On the other hand, the detection of Hz and CO in air ambient is through a reaction with the extrinsic states associated with the chemisorbed oxygen ions. The catalyst layer and adsorptive oxide employed in the Catalyst - Adsorptive Oxide - Semiconductor MIS structure play an important role in gas selectivity, sensitivity, and enhance the devices to operate at much lower temperature than the conventional solid state gas detectors. This report presents data on the devices adsorption characteristics, activation energies for gases adsorption, and electro-induced gases adsorption properties for the family of gaseous sensors fabricated with various catalysts and adsorptive oxides.

Blue Laser Diodes And Leds Based On II-VI Semiconductor Heterostructures
abstract: We report the first observation of blue stimulated emission from a semiconductor laser structure. At 77K, under pulsed current injection, the laser devices output light in the blue spectral region at wavelengths as short as 475.4 nm (2.606 eV). This is the shortest wavelength ever generated by a semiconductor diode laser. LEDs have also been fabricated which emit bright blue light (dominant wavelength as short as 479 nm) at room temperature. The p-on-n heterostructure LEDs exhibit excellent electrical properties as well: Mesa devices produce 25 mA at 4.4 V at 300K. Green and blue/green LEDs have also been fabricated and studied. It is our intention to report accurate LED efficiencies over the temperature range 77-300K. Results of these experiments, and additional laser diode experiments which are in progress, will also be presented and discussed.

Design of Current Sensors in IGBT's
abstract: The operation of current sensors (or pilots) in insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) is described for the first time experimentally and with two-dimensional simulations. Two different sensor structures are compared. In the most conventional structure, a small IGBT, separated from the main device by metallization only, is used as a current sensor (or pilot) and the emitter of this small IGBT is connected to ground via a resistor As the voltage at the emitter of the current sensor increases due to increasing current flow, the forward drop across the current sensor decreases and the ratio between the main current to the sensor current decreases. Experimentally, the dependence of the normalized current-sensor (or pilot) voltage (V<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">p</sub>) on the main IGBT current of a 500 V, n-channel, asymmetric IGBT bas been shown to be fairly linear, except when a small main current or a large pilot resistor is used. The main-to-pilot current ratio increases with increasing carrier lifetime and increasing distance from the main IGBT. Also, during IGBT turn-off, the current and voltage in the current sensor tends to lead, due to lesser RC delay, the main device. This could lead to latchup or loss of gate control in the current sensor path. To avoid this problem, a different type of current sensor is designed and characterized. The n+ source diffusion is removed from the current sensor area and hence the MOS channel current as well as the parasitic thyristor is removed. This current sensor only collects the minority carriers (holes here) injected from the p+ substrate. However, it has more non-linearities in its current ratio when compared to the conventional structure. The usage range of the current-sensor voltage can be obtained by examining I<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pE</sub> vs V<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">p</sub>.

Milliampere-range "twice-buried" AlGaAs-heterolasers Fabricated By Low Temperature Liquid Phase Epitaxy
abstract: The present summary is concerned with low threshold quantum well AlGaAs-heterolasers emitting at wavelengths 730-850 nm. A special LPE (Liquid Phase Epitaxy) technique has been developed to crystallize thin layer AlGaAs-heterostructures in the low temperature range of 600-400°C. We have developed "twice-buried" stripe laser heterostructures to considerably narrow down the width of the current channel, to confine the optical mode in lateral directions and to compensate for the strain tensions in the active layer in order to solve the laser lifetime problem. Such structure was fabricated by three LPE processes. At first, a planar quantum well separate confinement laser heterostructure was grown by low-temperature LPE. The simple and cheap LPE technique developed is promising to grow not only laser structures, but structures of HEMTs, photocells with ultra-thin windows and others.
